Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Learning from a closed case

Once a safeguarding case formally closes, whether through a satisfactory resolution or a determination that the original concern was unfounded, the case is briefly reviewed for any genuine learning about how the suite's procedures functioned in practice, distinct from the outcome itself, since even a case that resolves well can still reveal a timing gap or communication issue worth addressing.

Confidentiality and information governance in a safeguarding case

Safeguarding information is held to the same confidentiality standard as any other resident record, accessed only by those with a genuine need to know as part of their role in the specific case, and never discussed informally outside that circle; this confidentiality standard sits alongside, and is never used to avoid, the duty to escalate and share information appropriately within the safeguarding process itself, including under the multi-agency information sharing appendix.

Handling an anonymous safeguarding concern

A concern raised anonymously, whether through the Whistleblowing Policy's own anonymous route or otherwise, is investigated with the same seriousness as a concern raised openly, since the value of the information itself does not depend on who raised it; this applies equally to an anonymous concern about self-neglect raised by, for example, a worried neighbour or visitor.

Reviewing this overarching policy's own effectiveness

Beyond the specific procedure reviews and the whole-suite audit, the Board periodically considers whether the safeguarding framework as a whole, including this overarching document's own structure, remains fit for purpose, informed by external benchmarking against sector guidance and any relevant regulatory feedback.

Preventing self-neglect through early identification

Regular, attentive contact with a resident is itself a preventive measure against self-neglect reaching a serious point unnoticed; staff are trained to notice a gradual change in a resident's self-care, mood, or engagement with their environment as early as possible, since intervening supportively at an early stage is both kinder to the resident and more effective than responding only once the situation has become significantly more serious.

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the safeguarding champion role at each Alderbridge site. It applies to every registered manager deciding who to nominate.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages a resident's personal money and, where
relevant, an appointeeship or deputyship arrangement. It applies to every site holding any resident funds
or acting under a financial authority on a resident's behalf.

Policy statement

A resident's money is handled with the same care and transparency Alderbridge would expect if it were its
own, with clear records and independent checks in place so that a resident, their family, and any external
body can be confident funds have been used only for the resident's own benefit.

Definitions

**Personal allowance** the resident's own spending money held by the site on their behalf.
**Appointeeship** the formal DWP arrangement allowing Alderbridge or an individual to manage a
resident's benefits on their behalf where they lack capacity to do so themselves. **Financial concern** any
observation suggesting a resident's money may have been mishandled, misused, or is otherwise
unaccounted for, now escalated as a safeguarding matter in the first instance.

Roles and responsibilities

**The registered manager** holds day-to-day oversight of resident funds at their site. **The Alderbridge
Safeguarding Lead** is now the escalation contact for a financial concern raised at any site, a change from
the previous version's Finance Manager route, and coordinates with the Finance Manager on the financial
record aspect once a concern is raised. **Care staff** record every transaction involving a resident's
personal allowance at the time it occurs, never relying on memory to reconstruct it later.

**Does every near miss need to be escalated to the Safeguarding Lead?** No, only where the incident itself, not merely its medication nature, raises a safeguarding concern such as a deliberate act or a pattern suggesting neglect; a genuine, isolated administration error follows the standard medication incident route. **Who decided to add the severity appendix?** The Quality Lead, following a medication audit that identified inconsistent escalation urgency across similarly severe incidents.

Training and competency

Medication competency training covers the severity appendix and the aligned safeguarding escalation route, alongside the specific policy relevant to a staff member's actual duties.

Monitoring and compliance

The Quality Lead reviews medication incident severity trends quarterly, coordinating with the Safeguarding Lead where a trend suggests a safeguarding dimension worth wider review.

Record keeping and retention

Records for each specific medication activity, including incident severity classifications, are retained per that activity's own policy and the Records Retention Schedule.

Approval and review history

This overarching policy was approved by the Chief Executive on 1 March 2025, this version took effect 1 November 2025 superseding the earlier version, and is due for review in November 2026.

How the suite is kept up to date

A specific medication policy is reviewed on its own cycle, but any change is also checked against this overarching document, its appendix tables, and the current safeguarding escalation standard to confirm consistency across the whole suite.

The legal basis for covert administration

Covert administration is only ever considered where a resident lacks the mental capacity to consent to taking their medication openly, following a formal capacity assessment under the Mental Capacity Act; it is never used for a capacitous resident who simply refuses medication. The best-interests decision involves the resident's family or advocate where available, the GP, and a pharmacist, and is recorded formally with a defined review date.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Learning from a serious case review

Post-breach review and organisational learning

Beyond the individual breach's own resolution, the Data Protection Lead reviews breach data quarterly for
any recurring type or cause, and a genuinely recurring pattern (for example, repeated misdirected emails
to a similarly named recipient) triggers a specific process or system change — for example, a mandatory
confirmation step before sending to an external address — rather than each individual recurrence simply
being logged and closed without addressing why it keeps happening.

Distinguishing a breach from an ordinary IT fault

Not every IT problem is a data breach; a system outage that prevents access to data, with no evidence
anyone unauthorised accessed or exfiltrated it, is handled under the IT Outage Contact Tree rather than
this procedure, though the Data Protection Lead is still briefed and remains alert to any sign the outage's
underlying cause might also have a data protection dimension that only becomes apparent as IT's own
investigation progresses.

Breach response outside normal working hours

A suspected breach discovered outside normal office hours is reported to the on-call manager, who
contacts the Data Protection Lead directly rather than the report waiting until the next working day, since
the 72-hour notification clock and the value of fast containment do not pause simply because the discovery
happened at a less convenient time.

Protection Lead** confirms the requester's identity and any authority claimed, coordinates gathering the relevant records across every system that might hold them, and completes any necessary redaction before disclosure. **Each registered manager and HR** supports the Data Protection Lead by identifying and providing the records held at their own site or function promptly when asked.

Confirm the request is genuinely a SAR (a request to see personal data), rather than a different kind of enquiry that might be better handled another way, though where genuinely unclear, treat it as a SAR by default.

Confirm the requester's identity and, where they are not the data subject themselves, their valid authority to receive the data subject's personal data.

Search every relevant system and paper record for personal data about the requester, not only the most obvious source (for example, the care record alone, when email correspondence might also be relevant).

Review every document found and redact any third-party personal data it contains, unless that third party has consented to its disclosure.

Prepare a response explaining what personal data is held, why it is processed, who it is shared with, and how long it is retained, alongside the actual data itself.

Respond within one calendar month of receipt, or explain in writing before that deadline why a genuinely complex request needs the further two-month extension this procedure allows, rather than simply missing the deadline without explanation.

Record the request and its outcome, including the time taken, so response-time compliance can be monitored across every SAR received.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where disclosing specific information would cause serious harm to the data subject's own physical or mental health (a narrow exemption available for health data specifically), the Data Protection Lead seeks a clinical opinion before deciding whether to withhold that specific element, and any such withholding is explained to the requester as far as possible without disclosing the harmful information itself, rather than used as a general excuse to withhold inconvenient information.

Local and regional variations

No local or regional variation applies; SAR handling is deliberately centralised through the Data Protection Lead regardless of which site the request relates to, to ensure a single consistent standard and a single point of accountability for the statutory timescale.

Where a data subject has been supported or employed at more than one Alderbridge site over time, the Data Protection Lead coordinates a single search across every relevant site and system rather than each site separately deciding what falls within scope, ensuring the eventual response is genuinely complete rather than reflecting only the most recent or most obvious location.

Extended frequently asked questions

**What if some of the requested data is held by a third-party data processor (for example, a payroll provider) rather than Alderbridge directly?** The Data Protection Lead requests the relevant data from that processor under the existing data processing agreement, since the data remains Alderbridge's own responsibility to disclose regardless of where it is technically stored. **Can a SAR be refused outright?** Only in narrow, specific circumstances set out in law (for example, where an exemption genuinely applies); a request is never simply refused because it is inconvenient or time-consuming to fulfil. **How is a SAR different from an ordinary request to update incorrect information?** The latter is a rectification request, handled under a related but distinct right; the Data Protection Lead confirms which right is actually being exercised and responds accordingly, since the two have different substantive requirements even though they are related.

Redaction in practice

Redacting third-party data is not simply blacking out a name; the Data Protection Lead considers whether the surrounding context would still make the third party identifiable even with their name removed (for example, 'the resident in the next room' in a small care home), and redacts or generalises accordingly, since a technically redacted but still practically identifying disclosure does not meet this procedure's own standard.

Handling a request that appears to be motivated by an unrelated dispute

Where a SAR appears to be made in the context of a separate dispute (for example, a family disagreement, or an ongoing complaint), it is still handled exactly as any other SAR would be, in full and within the same timescale, since the requester's motivation for exercising their legal right does not change the right itself or Alderbridge's obligation to respond to it properly.

Purpose and scope

This overarching policy sets out the framework of safeguarding-related policies and procedures at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every site and signposts the more detailed policy or procedure governing each specific safeguarding situation.

Policy statement

Safeguarding at Alderbridge follows a consistent set of principles across every specific policy in this area, now including self-neglect as a signposted concern, a multi-agency information sharing appendix, and terminology aligned throughout to 'Safeguarding Champion'.

Definitions

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Learning from a closed case

Once a safeguarding case formally closes, whether through a satisfactory resolution or a determination that the original concern was unfounded, the case is briefly reviewed for any genuine learning about how the suite's procedures functioned in practice, distinct from the outcome itself, since even a case that resolves well can still reveal a timing gap or communication issue worth addressing.

Confidentiality and information governance in a safeguarding case

Safeguarding information is held to the same confidentiality standard as any other resident record, accessed only by those with a genuine need to know as part of their role in the specific case, and never discussed informally outside that circle; this confidentiality standard sits alongside, and is never used to avoid, the duty to escalate and share information appropriately within the safeguarding process itself, including under the multi-agency information sharing appendix.

Handling an anonymous safeguarding concern

A concern raised anonymously, whether through the Whistleblowing Policy's own anonymous route or otherwise, is investigated with the same seriousness as a concern raised openly, since the value of the information itself does not depend on who raised it; this applies equally to an anonymous concern about self-neglect raised by, for example, a worried neighbour or visitor.

Reviewing this overarching policy's own effectiveness

Beyond the specific procedure reviews and the whole-suite audit, the Board periodically considers whether the safeguarding framework as a whole, including this overarching document's own structure, remains fit for purpose, informed by external benchmarking against sector guidance and any relevant regulatory feedback.

Preventing self-neglect through early identification

Regular, attentive contact with a resident is itself a preventive measure against self-neglect reaching a serious point unnoticed; staff are trained to notice a gradual change in a resident's self-care, mood, or engagement with their environment as early as possible, since intervening supportively at an early stage is both kinder to the resident and more effective than responding only once the situation has become significantly more serious.

First Aid Provision: Who to Contact

Purpose and scope

This guidance sets out first aid provision at every Alderbridge site. It applies to every shift, ensuring appropriate first aid cover is always available.

Policy statement

Every shift has access to a trained first aider and a stocked first aid box, so that an injury to a resident, staff member or visitor can be responded to promptly and competently.

Definitions

**First aider** a staff member holding a current first aid at work qualification. **Appointed person** a staff member responsible for calling emergency services and looking after first aid equipment, where a full first aider is not required by the site's risk assessment. **First aid box** the stocked, clearly labelled box maintained at each site.

1. Ensure at least one qualified first aider is on duty for every shift, based on the site's own risk assessment of resident numbers and needs.
2. Check the first aid box monthly, restocking any used or expired item promptly.
3. Record every first aid incident, however minor, in the accident book kept alongside the first aid box.
4. Call emergency services immediately for any injury beyond what first aid can safely manage.

Policy statement

3. Support the safeguarding champion to attend the wider Alderbridge safeguarding network meeting, sharing learning across sites.
4. Arrange cover for the safeguarding champion role during their absence, so the first point of contact function is never left unfilled.

Worked example

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

Purpose and scope

Policy statement

Each site nominates a safeguarding champion who acts as the first point of contact for safeguarding questions, providing local expertise and support to colleagues raising a concern.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. 2. The registered manager contacts the LADO the same working day the allegation becomes known, a

Safeguarding Training Levels: Who Needs What

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the different levels of safeguarding training required across Alderbridge roles. It applies to every member of staff and every registered manager.

Policy statement

Safeguarding training is matched to a role's actual level of resident contact and responsibility, so that every staff member holds the depth of training genuinely relevant to their duties.

Definitions

**Level 1** basic safeguarding awareness, required for every member of staff regardless of role. **Level 2** intermediate training for a role with direct, regular resident contact. **Level 3** advanced training for a registered manager, deputy, or designated Safeguarding Champion.

1. Complete Level 1 safeguarding awareness training as part of induction, regardless of role.
2. Complete Level 2 training within the first month for any role involving direct, regular resident contact.
3. Complete Level 3 training before taking on a registered manager, deputy, or Safeguarding Champion role.
4. Refresh the applicable level every three years, or sooner if guidance changes significantly.

*Supersedes the version effective 1 June 2025. 'Safeguarding lead' renamed to 'Safeguarding champion' throughout — the role and its responsibilities are unchanged.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the safeguarding champion role at each Alderbridge site. It applies to every registered manager deciding who to nominate.

Policy statement

Each site nominates a safeguarding champion who acts as the first point of contact for safeguarding questions, providing local expertise and support to colleagues raising a concern.

Definitions

**Safeguarding champion** the Level 3 trained staff member nominated at each site as the local point of safeguarding expertise, renamed in this version from the previous term 'safeguarding lead' — the role itself is unchanged. **First point of contact** the role of being the person a colleague approaches first with a safeguarding question or concern, before wider escalation.

1. Nominate a staff member holding, or willing to complete, Level 3 safeguarding training as the site's safeguarding champion.
2. Make the safeguarding champion's identity clearly known to every staff member, including on the site's safeguarding noticeboard, updated to reflect the new title.
3. Support the safeguarding champion to attend the wider Alderbridge safeguarding network meeting, sharing learning across sites.
4. Arrange cover for the safeguarding champion role during their absence, so the first point of contact function is never left unfilled.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the Adult Safeguarding Policy (the wider framework the safeguarding champion supports) and the Safeguarding Training Levels Guidance (governing the Level 3 training this role requires).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates that only the title has changed. A care assistant notices something that concerns them but is unsure whether it meets the safeguarding referral threshold. They raise it informally with the site's safeguarding champion, who provides the same experienced first-point-of-contact support the role always has, under its new name.

Frequently asked questions

A worked example illustrates that only the title has changed. A care assistant notices something that concerns them but is unsure whether it meets the safeguarding referral threshold. They raise it informally with the site's safeguarding champion, who provides the same experienced first-point-of-contact support the role always has, under its new name.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the role renamed?** A review found 'champion' better reflects the role's supportive, promotional nature within the site, whereas 'lead' was sometimes mistaken for a formal management title; the responsibilities themselves have not changed. **Does a site need to re-nominate its safeguarding champion following the rename?** No, an existing safeguarding lead simply continues under the new title without needing to be re-nominated or retrained.

Reviewing the nomination periodically

The registered manager reviews the safeguarding champion nomination annually, or sooner if the current post-holder moves role or leaves, confirming the site always has a clearly identified, currently-trained person filling this function under its current title rather than an outdated name remaining on the noticeboard.

Closing note

Having a known, approachable local expert makes a colleague more likely to raise an early concern, and this guidance exists to make that role a genuine, visible presence at every site, under whichever name it is known by.

Purpose and scope

This overarching policy sets out the framework of safeguarding-related policies and procedures at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every site and signposts the more detailed policy or procedure governing each specific safeguarding situation.

Policy statement

Safeguarding at Alderbridge follows a consistent set of principles across every specific policy in this area, now including self-neglect as a signposted concern, a multi-agency information sharing appendix, and terminology aligned throughout to 'Safeguarding Champion'.

Definitions

**The safeguarding policy suite** the full set of specific policies and procedures this overarching document signposts, including allegations against staff, missing person, body mapping, resident finances, and now self-neglect. **Safeguarding Champion** the site-level role providing local safeguarding expertise, using the term adopted when the role was renamed from 'safeguarding lead' at site level; this overarching document's own terminology is aligned to match in this version. **Self-neglect** a resident's own inability or unwillingness to care for themselves or their environment to a degree that risks their health or safety, now explicitly recognised within this suite. **Multi-agency information sharing** the principles governing what safeguarding information Alderbridge shares with an external agency such as the local authority or police.

Safeguarding Adults Board engagement

Alderbridge participates in the relevant local authority's Safeguarding Adults Board where a site's residents fall within that authority's area, contributing to multi-agency learning and receiving updates on local safeguarding priorities; the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead represents Alderbridge at this Board.

The role of an advocate

Where a resident lacks capacity to fully participate in a safeguarding process, or would benefit from independent support regardless of capacity, an independent advocate is arranged to represent the resident's own wishes and interests throughout the process, distinct from a family member's role.

Whole-suite training pathway

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the different levels of safeguarding training required across Alderbridge roles. It applies to every member of staff and every registered manager.

Policy statement

Safeguarding training is matched to a role's actual level of resident contact and responsibility, so that every staff member holds the depth of training genuinely relevant to their duties.

Definitions

Worked example

Purpose and scope

This overarching policy sets out the framework of safeguarding-related policies and procedures at Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every site and signposts the more detailed policy or procedure governing each specific safeguarding situation.

Policy statement

Safeguarding at Alderbridge follows a consistent set of principles across every specific policy in this area, now including self-neglect as a signposted concern, a multi-agency information sharing appendix, and terminology aligned throughout to 'Safeguarding Champion'.

Definitions

**The safeguarding policy suite** the full set of specific policies and procedures this overarching document signposts, including allegations against staff, missing person, body mapping, resident finances, and now self-neglect. **Safeguarding Champion** the site-level role providing local safeguarding expertise, using the term adopted when the role was renamed from 'safeguarding lead' at site level; this overarching document's own terminology is aligned to match in this version. **Self-neglect** a resident's own inability or unwillingness to care for themselves or their environment to a degree that risks their health or safety, now explicitly recognised within this suite. **Multi-agency information sharing** the principles governing what safeguarding information Alderbridge shares with an external agency such as the local authority or police.

Safeguarding Adults Board engagement

Alderbridge participates in the relevant local authority's Safeguarding Adults Board where a site's residents fall within that authority's area, contributing to multi-agency learning and receiving updates on local safeguarding priorities; the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead represents Alderbridge at this Board.

The role of an advocate

Where a resident lacks capacity to fully participate in a safeguarding process, or would benefit from independent support regardless of capacity, an independent advocate is arranged to represent the resident's own wishes and interests throughout the process, distinct from a family member's role.

Historical development of the safeguarding suite

The safeguarding policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single general safeguarding policy that, as specific situation types proved to need more detailed guidance, was gradually expanded into the distinct specific procedures this overarching document now signposts. Self-neglect's formal addition in this version continues that same pattern.

The six safeguarding principles

Alderbridge's safeguarding practice is grounded in the six nationally recognised safeguarding principles: empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership, and accountability. A self-neglect situation, in particular, calls empowerment and proportionality sharply into focus, since respecting a capacitous resident's own choice while still exercising a genuine duty of care requires balancing these principles carefully rather than defaulting reflexively to either extreme.

Resident voice in the safeguarding process

Wherever a resident is able to participate, their own wishes and views are sought and given real weight throughout a safeguarding process, not merely noted as a formality; this is especially central to a self-neglect situation, where the resident's own account of their choices and priorities is the starting point for any supportive response.

Handling a concern about a visitor or family member

A safeguarding concern is not limited to staff conduct; where a visitor or family member's behaviour raises a concern, the same escalation principles apply, coordinated where relevant with the Visiting Arrangements Policy's own provision for a documented, resident-specific restriction where a genuine safeguarding reason requires one.

Cross-border and out-of-area considerations

Where a resident's safeguarding history involves a local authority area outside where their current Alderbridge site sits, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead liaises with the originating authority to ensure relevant history transfers appropriately, using the multi-agency information sharing principles this version formalises.

Learning from a serious case review

Where Alderbridge is involved in, or a sector-wide serious case review identifies a lesson relevant to, a serious safeguarding failure, the Safeguarding Lead ensures that lesson is considered against this overarching policy and its suite, with any resulting change tracked and communicated to staff.

Supporting a staff member involved in a difficult safeguarding case

A staff member closely involved in a distressing safeguarding case, whether as the person who raised the concern or as part of the response, is offered support similar to that available following a resident's death, recognising that safeguarding work, including a self-neglect case that can be particularly difficult to sit with, is emotionally demanding even when handled well.

Auditing the suite as a whole

Beyond auditing each specific procedure on its own terms, the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead conducts an annual whole-suite audit, sampling a cross-section of cases across every specific safeguarding procedure to confirm the suite functions coherently for a situation genuinely spanning several of its specific procedures at once.

*Supersedes the version effective 1 June 2025. 'Safeguarding lead' renamed to 'Safeguarding champion' throughout — the role and its responsibilities are unchanged.*

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains the safeguarding champion role at each Alderbridge site. It applies to every registered manager deciding who to nominate.

Policy statement

Each site nominates a safeguarding champion who acts as the first point of contact for safeguarding questions, providing local expertise and support to colleagues raising a concern.

Definitions

**Safeguarding champion** the Level 3 trained staff member nominated at each site as the local point of safeguarding expertise, renamed in this version from the previous term 'safeguarding lead' — the role itself is unchanged. **First point of contact** the role of being the person a colleague approaches first with a safeguarding question or concern, before wider escalation.

1. Nominate a staff member holding, or willing to complete, Level 3 safeguarding training as the site's safeguarding champion.
2. Make the safeguarding champion's identity clearly known to every staff member, including on the site's safeguarding noticeboard, updated to reflect the new title.
3. Support the safeguarding champion to attend the wider Alderbridge safeguarding network meeting, sharing learning across sites.
4. Arrange cover for the safeguarding champion role during their absence, so the first point of contact function is never left unfilled.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the Adult Safeguarding Policy (the wider framework the safeguarding champion supports) and the Safeguarding Training Levels Guidance (governing the Level 3 training this role requires).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates that only the title has changed. A care assistant notices something that concerns them but is unsure whether it meets the safeguarding referral threshold. They raise it informally with the site's safeguarding champion, who provides the same experienced first-point-of-contact support the role always has, under its new name.

Frequently asked questions

A worked example illustrates that only the title has changed. A care assistant notices something that concerns them but is unsure whether it meets the safeguarding referral threshold. They raise it informally with the site's safeguarding champion, who provides the same experienced first-point-of-contact support the role always has, under its new name.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the role renamed?** A review found 'champion' better reflects the role's supportive, promotional nature within the site, whereas 'lead' was sometimes mistaken for a formal management title; the responsibilities themselves have not changed. **Does a site need to re-nominate its safeguarding champion following the rename?** No, an existing safeguarding lead simply continues under the new title without needing to be re-nominated or retrained.

Reviewing the nomination periodically

The registered manager reviews the safeguarding champion nomination annually, or sooner if the current post-holder moves role or leaves, confirming the site always has a clearly identified, currently-trained person filling this function under its current title rather than an outdated name remaining on the noticeboard.

Closing note

Having a known, approachable local expert makes a colleague more likely to raise an early concern, and this guidance exists to make that role a genuine, visible presence at every site, under whichever name it is known by.

Allegation against staff	Allegations Against Staff Procedure	Registered manager, then LADO

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a concern does not clearly fall under one of the suite's individual procedures, staff escalate under the general Adult Safeguarding Policy route immediately and let the registered manager or Safeguarding Champion determine which specific procedure, if any, additionally applies.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This overarching policy sits above the full safeguarding policy suite and now explicitly incorporates the multi-agency information sharing principles previously handled inconsistently on a case-by-case basis.

Why self-neglect was added

A review found staff were unsure how to respond when a resident with capacity chose to live in a way that raised health or safety concerns, such as declining support with personal care to a degree affecting their wellbeing; the new Self-Neglect Guidance gives a clear, respectful framework balancing a resident's autonomy against a genuine duty of care.

Why terminology was aligned to Safeguarding Champion

Following the site-level role's rename from 'safeguarding lead' to 'Safeguarding Champion', this overarching document's own references were inconsistent with the current title; this version aligns terminology throughout to avoid a reader being confused about whether 'safeguarding lead' meant the site role or the organisation-level role, which retains a distinct title.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates self-neglect and the terminology alignment together. A resident with full capacity is declining support with personal hygiene to a degree affecting their skin health. The site Safeguarding Champion is consulted per the new Self-Neglect Guidance, working with the GP and multidisciplinary team to support the resident's own choice as far as possible while addressing the genuine health risk, and information about the situation is shared with the resident's GP per the multi-agency information sharing appendix's proportionality principle.

Frequently asked questions

**Does self-neglect override a resident's right to make their own choices?** No, the guidance is designed to respect a capacitous resident's autonomy while still offering support and monitoring a genuine health risk; it is not a route to override a lawful choice. **Why does the organisation still have two different safeguarding-titled roles?** The site-level Safeguarding Champion provides local, everyday expertise, while the organisation-level Safeguarding Lead oversees the whole suite and coordinates cross-site and multi-agency matters; the titles are now kept clearly distinct throughout this document.

Training and competency

Safeguarding training at every level introduces this overarching policy, its appendices, and the current Safeguarding Champion terminology, with the specific procedure relevant to a staff member's actual duties covered in more depth.

Monitoring and compliance

The organisation-level Safeguarding Lead reviews practice across the whole suite quarterly, including self-neglect cases and multi-agency information sharing decisions.

Record keeping and retention

Records for each specific safeguarding situation, including a self-neglect case and any information shared with an external agency, are retained per that situation's own procedure and the Records Retention Schedule.

Approval and review history

This overarching policy was approved by the Chief Executive on 1 March 2025, this version took effect 1 January 2026 superseding the earlier version, and is due for review in January 2027.
